LESSON 1 · KEY CONCEPT📖 p. 74
Slide 6 / 34
The Five Levels of Organization
From smallest to largest — each level contains the one before it.
LESSON 1 · BUILDING UP📖 p. 74
Slide 7 / 34
Level 1 → Level 2
POPULATION = all members of the SAME species in an area at the same time. The key word is same species.
LESSON 1 · DEFINITION📖 p. 74
Slide 8 / 34
What Is a Species?
FERTILE means the offspring can grow up and have babies of their own. A horse and a donkey can have a mule — but the mule is sterile. So horses and donkeys are different species.
LESSON 1 · BUILDING UP📖 p. 74
Slide 9 / 34
Level 2 → Level 3: Community
COMMUNITY = all the populations of DIFFERENT species living together in the same area at the same time.
LESSON 1 · KEY CONCEPT📖 p. 74–75
Slide 10 / 34
Level 3 → Level 4: Ecosystem
ECOSYSTEM = a community (BIOTIC) + the non-living things around it (ABIOTIC). Both are needed!
LESSON 1 · TOP LEVEL📖 p. 74
Slide 11 / 34
Level 5: The Biosphere
BIOSPHERE = ALL ecosystems on Earth + the surrounding atmosphere. Every place where life is found.

From Levels to Limits
✓ WHAT WE LEARNED

Lesson 1 — Levels of Organization

  • Living things are organized in 5 levels: individual → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere
  • Biotic = living things; abiotic = non-living things — both are part of an ecosystem
  • A species is defined by being able to produce fertile offspring
  • The Etosha animals share resources at one big watering hole community
→ COMING UP NEXT

Lesson 2 — Resources & Populations

  • If resources at the watering hole run out, what happens to the animals?
  • We'll learn the 5 limiting factors that restrict how big a population can grow
  • And explore the most a population can ever reach: carrying capacity
LESSON 2 · pp. 76–80
Resources & Populations
How big can populations get? What stops them from growing forever?
💧 5 limiting factors 🐹 Pika Predicaments 📈 Carrying Capacity 🚨 Endangered Species
🔗 Builds on Lesson 1: Levels of Organization
LESSON 2 · KEY CONCEPT📖 p. 77
Slide 16 / 34
What Is a Limiting Factor?
A LIMITING FACTOR is anything that restricts the size of a population.
LESSON 2 · INVESTIGATION📖 p. 78
Slide 17 / 34
Pika Predicaments
A real population of pikas faces ALL 5 limiting factors at once. Find each one in the picture.
LESSON 2 · LAB MODEL📖 p. 76
Slide 18 / 34
Fishy Population Lab — How Space Limits Growth
The pond can only hold 16 fish. Even though the population doubles each generation, it cannot grow past 16 — the pond has reached its carrying capacity.
LESSON 2 · KEY GRAPH📖 p. 79
Slide 19 / 34
Biotic Potential vs Carrying Capacity
Biotic potential = how big a population could grow with NO limits. Almost never happens in real life.
Carrying capacity = the LARGEST population an ecosystem can actually support over time.
LESSON 2 · WHEN POPULATIONS GET TOO BIG📖 p. 79
Slide 20 / 34
Overpopulation: A Chain Reaction
OVERPOPULATION happens when a population grows so large it damages its own ecosystem — and hurts other populations too.
LESSON 2 · GOING THE OTHER WAY📖 p. 80
Slide 21 / 34
Why Populations Shrink
Populations DON'T always grow. They can shrink quickly because of seasonal changes or natural disasters.
LESSON 2 · POPULATION STATUS📖 p. 80
Slide 22 / 34
Threatened → Endangered → Extinct
From at-risk to gone forever — three categories of population status (IUCN Red List).

From Theory to a Real Crisis
✓ WHAT WE LEARNED

Lesson 2 — Resources & Populations

  • 5 limiting factors: water, food, sunlight, temperature, space
  • Biotic potential = max growth in perfect conditions; carrying capacity = realistic max
  • Overpopulation damages ecosystems — and hurts other species
  • Threatened → Endangered → Extinct show how populations can collapse
→ COMING UP NEXT

Lesson 3 — California Drought Case Study

  • What happens when a real, modern ecosystem loses its water?
  • We'll look at the 2011–2014 California drought — the worst on record
  • Then practice predicting chain reactions with prairie grass and deer

Coyote Population Analysis
Q2. A population of coyotes lives in a habitat with plentiful food and no predators. At the 1-year mark, what is happening to the population?
A. The population size is increasing.
B. The population size is decreasing.
C. The population size is remaining the same.
D. Cannot be inferred from the graph.
Q3. When the population reached its carrying capacity, what happened, and why?
A. Continued increasing — ecosystem hadn't changed.
B. Stopped increasing — reached the largest number the ecosystem could support.
C. Became zero — ecosystem could no longer support coyotes.
D. Cannot be inferred from the graph.
